Now I can read the contradiction precisely. "Green" in Settings means: device UUID present, notification key present, APNs token present, pinned hosts listed, and **`recent_failures` empty** — that last field is read from the breadcrumb slot the extension writes. And your banner text ("Couldn't verify…") is a string **only the extension itself renders** — the server-side placeholder iOS would show if the extension never ran says "Custos / Encrypted notification" instead.

So the extension *is* running and rendering its notice — but through a path that leaves no breadcrumb. Reading the Swift, there are exactly two such paths:

1. **The timeout path** (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`): iOS gave the extension its time budget, resolution didn't finish, iOS force-delivers — the code writes the notice but (unlike the normal failure path) records **no breadcrumb**. That's a genuine diagnostic blind spot regardless of anything else.
2. **A both-ways-broken keychain**: if the extension's process can't reach the shared access group at all, the key/pin *reads* come back nil (→ notice) *and* the breadcrumb *write* fails silently (→ green Settings). One cause, both symptoms. Your app-side keychain is provably fine (Settings shows the key id and pinned hosts), so this would specifically be an app↔extension entitlement mismatch in the built product.

Two observations from your side will split these cleanly:

- **Timing**: after the login page shows the number, does the banner appear **immediately** or with a **noticeable ~30-second lag**? A lag is the timeout path's signature; instant means the keychain story.
- **Tap behavior**: verified payloads carry a deep-link route; unverified ones deliberately don't. (Expected: tapping just opens the app — confirming it does rules out any half-verified weirdness.)

Meanwhile, the blind spot is a fact of the code regardless of your root cause, so I'm filing it:

input.title: NSE timeout path renders the unverified notice without recording a breadcrumb — Settings stays green while banners say "couldn't verify"
input.description:
## Symptom

Observed live 2026-07-29 during the first production push-to-approve exercise: every push renders the "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance" banner, while Settings → Notifications reports zero recent failures (green). The diagnostics surface exists precisely to explain that banner, and in this state it silently contradicts it.

## Mechanism

`ios/NotificationService/NotificationService.swift` has two paths that render the unverified notice **without** writing a breadcrumb:

1. `serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire()` — the timeout path substitutes the notice and strips the sealed block, but never calls `NotifyBreadcrumbs.record`. Every timed-out push is invisible to Settings.
2. The `mutableCopy` platform-contract guard at the top of `didReceive` (deliberate, documented — probably fine to leave).

There is also a structural blind spot shared by all breadcrumbs: if the extension cannot reach the shared keychain access group at all, the key/pin reads fail (→ notice via `.unverified(.openFailed)`) and the `NotifyBreadcrumbs.record` write fails just as silently (→ green Settings). A fully broken app↔extension keychain contract is therefore indistinguishable from perfect health in the one place built to explain it.

## Fix directions

- Record a `.timedOut` (or equivalent) breadcrumb in `serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire` before substituting the notice — the write is cheap and last-gasp-safe (delete-then-add under AfterFirstUnlock).
- Consider a sentinel the app can check for the keychain-broken case: e.g. the extension writes a tiny "extension ran at <ts>" heartbeat on every invocation; Settings showing "notices rendered but the extension has never checked in" converts the silent contradiction into a named diagnosis. (The app can compare against `UNUserNotificationCenter` delivered notifications carrying the unverified title.)

## Context

Found while diagnosing production pushes that render unverified with green diagnostics on the newest TestFlight build — root cause of that incident may be the timeout path itself or the keychain mismatch; this issue covers the observability gap that made the two indistinguishable. Related: MM-492 (handle rotation).

content.text:
[MM-493](https://linear.app/malpercio/issue/MM-493/nse-timeout-path-renders-the-unverified-notice-without-recording-a) is filed for the observability gap.

So, the two questions that crack your case open:

1. **How fast does the banner land** after the login page shows the number — instant, or a ~30-second lag? Lag = the extension is timing out (something in it stalls); instant = the extension fails fast, which combined with green Settings points at the app↔extension keychain contract being broken in the built product (reads *and* the breadcrumb write both failing).
2. **What happens when you tap it** — expected is "just opens the app" (unverified payloads deliberately carry no deep-link route).

If it turns out to be the instant/keychain flavor, the next place to look isn't the repo's source (the template and gates enforce the entitlements) but the **built artifact**: whether the App Store/TestFlight-signed extension actually carries `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` as its first (and only) keychain access group — i.e., whether the NSE's brand-new provisioning profile from today grants the keychain-sharing entitlement at all. A profile that omits it would sign and install cleanly and produce exactly this: an extension that runs, sees an empty keychain, renders the notice, and can't leave a trace.

The banner is generally slow, however I had one instant delivery. I couldn't promise you that it wasn't just an older delivery that happened to coincide with another login attempt, however. Tapping just opens the app.

That tap behavior is as designed (no route on unverified), and the timing answer is genuinely useful even though it doesn't fully split the fork: "generally slow" fits the timeout path, but APNs delivery jitter can also *look* like extension slowness from the outside — your one instant delivery proves the pipe can be fast, which keeps both theories alive. Remote analysis has hit its ceiling; the next instrument is your Mac, and it will settle this in one capture.

**The definitive test — Console.app against the extension (2 minutes):**

1. iPhone connected via USB, open **Console.app**, select the phone in the sidebar, filter on `NotificationService` (the extension's process name), press Start.
2. Trigger one push-to-approve, watch for ~40 seconds.
3. What you'll see, by cause:
   - **Keychain entitlement broken**: `SecItemCopyMatching` failures with **`-34018` (errSecMissingEntitlement)** or "no access group" chatter from the extension's PID the moment it launches. That's the smoking gun for the app↔extension access-group mismatch.
   - **Timeout**: the extension launches, goes quiet, and ~30s later `usernotificationsd`/`SpringBoard` logs an "extension took too long / expiring" message. Where it went quiet (right after launch vs. mid-work) narrows what's stalling.
   - **Crash/jetsam**: a crash report line — though that would render the "Custos / Encrypted notification" placeholder, not your notice, so I don't expect this one.

**In parallel, one static check on the built product** — whether the shipped extension actually carries the shared keychain group. Build the IPA locally and inspect the `.appex`:

```bash
just ios-ipa
```

then unzip the resulting `.ipa` and run:

```bash
codesign -d --entitlements :- "Payload/Obsign.app/PlugIns/NotificationService.appex"
```

Expected: `keychain-access-groups` containing exactly one entry, `<TeamID>.org.obsign.shared`. If that array is missing or empty in the signed product, the provisioning profile minted today for the NSE App ID doesn't grant Keychain Sharing — it would sign, install, and run exactly like this: extension alive, keychain invisible, notice rendered, no trace. (The repo's template gates check the *source* entitlements; the profile is the one link they can't see.)

Either finding gives us a one-move fix: `-34018`/missing entitlement → enable Keychain Sharing on the NSE App ID in the portal, regenerate its provisioning profile, update the CI secret, push a build; a clean entitlement + timeout signature → we instrument the extension (MM-493's breadcrumb-on-timeout plus a stopwatch breadcrumb) and hunt the stall with real data.

This log is decisive — and it kills the timeout theory outright:

```
19:50:05.236  Extension started, scheduled timers: serviceTime=29.678327
19:50:05.261  Service extension delivered mutated content
```

The extension launched, did its whole job, and delivered in **25 milliseconds**. No timeout, no crash, no memory kill. It ran the `.unverified` path at full speed — which means it *did* attempt the breadcrumb write. And Settings still shows green.

That leaves exactly one consistent story: **the extension's keychain is a different keychain than the app's.** With no explicit access group, reads search only the groups the *process* is entitled to, and writes land in its *first* entitled group. If the built appex is missing the shared `org.obsign.shared` group, everything behaves with no errors anywhere: the extension can't see the app's key/pins (→ every open fails → notice), its breadcrumb write *succeeds* into its own private group (→ no error), and the app reads its own groups (→ no failures → green). Silent on every side — the exact failure the repo's checks exist to prevent in *source*, now apparently present in the *built product*. Let me check what the template actually gives the NSE:

the app obtains the device token, the extension only decrypts what arrives. And no iCloud
    container: the extension touches no backup.

    PORTAL WORK: an app extension is a separate bundle
    (dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService), so it needs its own explicit App ID
    and its own distribution profile before the TestFlight lane can sign a build that embeds
    it. `keychain-access-groups` itself needs no registration — a provisioning profile
    authorizes the whole team prefix via a <TeamID>.* wildcard. See docs/ios-cicd.md.
  -->
  <key>keychain-access-groups</key>
  <array>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared</string>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>
</dict>
</plist>
=== app ===
    Neither entry may be removed or reordered while any install may still hold items in
    the legacy group. `just bundle-identity-check` and keychain.rs's
    `entitlement_declares_stable_group_first` test enforce both.

    UNLIKE the iCloud container above, this needs no Apple Developer portal registration:
    `keychain-access-groups` is not an App ID capability, and a provisioning profile already
    authorizes the entire team prefix through a `<TeamID>.*` wildcard — which is why
    `org.obsign.shared` signs fine while the bundle id is still `dev.malpercio.*`. Confirm
    after any profile change with:
      security cms -D -i <profile>.mobileprovision | plutil -p - | grep -A3 keychain-access-groups
  -->
  <key>keychain-access-groups</key>
  <array>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared</string>
    <string>$(AppIdentifierPrefix)dev.malpercio.identitywallet</string>
  </array>

  <!--
    Push notifications. Without this key `registerForRemoteNotifications` never yields a device
    token — it calls back with an error instead — so the whole notification-relay path is inert.
    The value selects which APNs environment the token is minted for; `development` is correct
    for debug builds and TestFlight, and Xcode's App Store export rewrites it to `production`.

    Like the iCloud container above (and UNLIKE keychain-access-groups), this DOES need Apple
    Developer portal work: enable the Push Notifications capability on the App ID and regenerate
    the provisioning profile, or signing fails with an entitlements mismatch. The official relay
    additionally needs an APNs auth key for this bundle id — that key is the structural reason a
    self-hoster cannot push directly and the relay exists at all.
  -->
  <key>aps-environment</key>
  <string>development</string>

content.text:
There it is, at the very bottom: 

```
error: exportArchive No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found
```

The whole picture snaps into focus:

**The wallet lane has been failing at the signing step since July 28** — the build compiles perfectly (the NSE appex builds, the archive completes), then export dies because the runner's keychain has no valid iOS Distribution certificate. Timing is telling: last green run 07-28 02:01, first failure 07-29 11:36 — right around the NSE App ID/provisioning portal work. The two classic causes: the distribution cert **expired** (they live one year), or it got **revoked/superseded** during that portal session and the new profiles now reference a cert that isn't the one stored in the CI secret.

**This also explains your device.** The build you're running can't be the 07-28 CI build — you have the Settings → Notifications section, which shipped with MM-420, and MM-420's CI build *failed*. So you're almost certainly on the locally-uploaded build from this morning's NSE-blocker verification — a snapshot of in-flight work, not current `main`. Debugging its NSE behavior any further is chasing a ghost: the decrypt-and-render code, entitlement resolution, and push-to-approve handling on `main` have all moved since.

**The path out (portal + secrets — yours, since it's all credential material):**

1. Apple Developer portal → **Certificates**: check the iOS/Apple Distribution cert's state. Expired or revoked → create a new **Apple Distribution** certificate, export it as `.p12`.
2. Regenerate **all three provisioning profiles** against the valid cert — wallet app, NSE (`dev.malpercio.identitywallet.NotificationService`), and admin-companion — since profiles bind to certs.
3. Update the GitHub Actions secrets: the cert `.p12` + password, and the three `IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_*` profiles.
4. Re-run the failed `ios-testflight` run (or I can trigger it once you say secrets are in) — it'll ship **current main**: v0.10.2 wallet with the final NSE, push-to-approve, everything.
5. Install that TestFlight build, open it once (re-register + re-pin), then one more push-to-approve.

The admin-companion lane shares the same cert secret, so expect it to need the same treatment. Let me record this so future sessions don't trust the "TestFlight is green" assumption:

**Route patterns:** see [[feedback_route_patterns]] — don't duplicate admin-token auth blocks / code generation / test utils; consolidate cross-table uniqueness checks with OR EXISTS.

# export costs seconds. This keeps the fix inside one recipe instead of forking the whole
# release lane away from tauri.
#
# No-ops for an app with no embedded extensions (admin-companion today), so both lanes share it.
_reexport-embedded-extensions app_dir:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    gen="{{app_dir}}/src-tauri/gen/apple"
    archive="$(ls -td "$gen"/build/*.xcarchive 2>/dev/null | head -n1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$archive" ]; then
      echo "✗ no .xcarchive under $gen/build — did the build actually run?" >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    app="$(ls -d "$archive"/Products/Applications/*.app 2>/dev/null | head -n1 || true)"
    if [ -z "$app" ]; then
      echo "✗ no .app inside $archive" >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    # Enumerate embedded bundles that need their own profile. Read from the archive rather than
    # assuming a name, so this keeps working if a second extension is ever added.
    appexes=()
    while IFS= read -r a; do [ -n "$a" ] && appexes+=("$a"); done < <(ls -d "$app"/PlugIns/*.appex 2>/dev/null || true)
    if [ "${#appexes[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
      echo "✓ no embedded extensions in $(basename "$app") — tauri's own export is complete"
      exit 0
    fi

    if [ -z "${IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE:-}" ]; then
      echo "✗ IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE is not set, but $(basename "$app") embeds an extension." >&2
      echo "  An app extension is a separate bundle and needs its OWN App Store provisioning" >&2
      echo "  profile, bound to its own App ID. Without it the extension ships with empty" >&2
      echo "  entitlements and App Store Connect rejects the upload." >&2
      echo "  Set it to the base64 of that .mobileprovision:" >&2
      echo "    export IOS_MOBILE_PROVISION_NSE=\"\$(base64 -i <profile>.mobileprovision)\"" >&2
      echo "  See docs/ios-cicd.md → \"Push notifications: three artifacts\"." >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    # Install the extension's profile where Xcode looks — the same folder and the same UUID
    # lookup tauri_macos_sign uses for the app's, so both are discoverable identically.
    profiles_dir="$HOME/Library/MobileDevice/Provisioning Profiles"
    mkdir -p "$profiles_dir"
    nse_profile="$(mktemp)"
    # `-d`, not `--decode`: both spellings work on the BSD base64 and the Nix GNU one this
    # repo can put ahead of it, but `-d` is the common denominator across older BSDs too.

# Make the distribution identity findable for THIS export. tauri imports IOS_CERTIFICATE
    # into an ephemeral keychain that is deleted the moment `cargo tauri ios build` exits, so
    # by the time this recipe runs, a fresh CI runner holds no signing identity at all and
    # `-exportArchive` fails with `No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found`. A
    # developer Mac hides this: the login keychain carries the same identity permanently,
    # which is why the lane can be red while the identical local build is green. Import into
    # our own temporary keychain, prepend it to the search list, and restore everything on
    # exit — the same lifecycle tauri gives its keychain, held open a recipe longer.
    reexport_keychain="$(mktemp -d)/reexport.keychain-db"
    cert_file="$(mktemp)"
    echo "$IOS_CERTIFICATE" | base64 -d > "$cert_file"
    prior_keychains=()
    while IFS= read -r k; do
      k="${k#"${k%%[![:space:]]*}"}"; k="${k%\"}"; k="${k#\"}"
      [ -n "$k" ] && prior_keychains+=("$k")
    done < <(security list-keychains -d user)
    restore_keychains() {
      security list-keychains -d user -s "${prior_keychains[@]}" 2>/dev/null || true
      security delete-keychain "$reexport_keychain" 2>/dev/null || true
    }
    trap restore_keychains EXIT
    security create-keychain -p "" "$reexport_keychain"
    security set-keychain-settings "$reexport_keychain"
    security unlock-keychain -p "" "$reexport_keychain"
    security import "$cert_file" -k "$reexport_keychain" \
      -P "${IOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD:-}" -T /usr/bin/codesign -T /usr/bin/security
    rm -f "$cert_file"
    # Without this, codesign under xcodebuild stalls on a keychain ACL prompt no CI can answer.
    security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple: -k "" "$reexport_keychain" >/dev/null
    security list-keychains -d user -s "$reexport_keychain" "${prior_keychains[@]}"

    echo "re-exporting $(basename "$archive") with profiles for every embedded bundle..."
    rm -f "$gen"/build/arm64/*.ipa
    xcodebuild -exportArchive \
      -archivePath "$archive" \
      -exportPath "$gen/build/arm64" \
      -exportOptionsPlist "$options" \
      -allowProvisioningUpdates >/dev/null
    rm -f "$options"

ios: give the embedded-extension re-export its own signing keychain

The re-export recipe runs xcodebuild -exportArchive after `cargo tauri
ios build` exits — but tauri imports IOS_CERTIFICATE into an ephemeral
keychain deleted when that process ends, so on a fresh CI runner the
second export finds no distribution identity and fails with
`No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found`. A developer Mac
masks this completely: the login keychain holds the same identity
permanently, so local builds pass while every CI run since the recipe
landed has failed at this step.

Import the certificate into a temporary keychain scoped to the recipe,
prepend it to the search list, and restore the prior list (deleting the
keychain) on exit. Skipped when IOS_CERTIFICATE is unset — the
standalone dev-Mac invocation, where the login keychain already serves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git push -u origin claude/reexport-keychain 2>&1 | tail -1 && gh pr create --title "ios: give the embedded-extension re-export its own signing keychain" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What

`_reexport-embedded-extensions` now imports `IOS_CERTIFICATE` into its own temporary keychain (search-list prepend, ACL partition list, full restore + delete on exit) before running its `xcodebuild -exportArchive`. Skipped when `IOS_CERTIFICATE` is unset (standalone dev-Mac use, where the login keychain already holds the identity).

## Why

Every wallet TestFlight run since 07-28 has failed at:

```
error: exportArchive No signing certificate "iOS Distribution" found
error: recipe `_reexport-embedded-extensions` failed with exit code 70
```

Root cause: tauri imports the distribution cert into an **ephemeral keychain torn down when `cargo tauri ios build` exits** (`tauri_macos_sign`). The re-export recipe — added with the NSE work, which is exactly when the lane went red — runs *after* that teardown, so a fresh runner holds no signing identity at all. A developer Mac masks the bug entirely (login keychain), which is why identical certificates "work locally": the certificate was never the problem, and rotating the secrets couldn't fix it.

Verified from tonight's re-run logs: secrets present and plausible (cert 4.4 KB b64, both profiles ~17-18 KB), tauri's own import reports "1 identity imported", the archive builds and signs — and the failure is precisely at the recipe's second export.

## Consequence of the outage

MM-420 (NSE decrypt-and-render), MM-443 (push-to-approve), and the v0.10.x wallet builds never shipped via CI — the installed TestFlight build is a locally-uploaded snapshot. Merging this re-triggers the lane (justfile/just/ios.just are in its `paths:`) and should ship current `main`.

## Verification

- `just -n` parse + `bash -n` of the rendered recipe body pass
- The keychain dance is the standard CI pattern (create → import → `set-key-partition-list` → search-list prepend → restore/delete on EXIT trap)
- Real proof requires the macOS lane itself — merging this runs it

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"
